components.gap: Pearl sec. 3.1, pp. 104-105, inside the cited secs. 3.1-3.2.3: in reading path diagrams the source uses the kinship relations parent, child, ancestor and descendant, and defines a path as any consecutive sequence of edges, solid or dashed, with the example that Fig. 1(b) has two paths between X and Y: the arrow X -> Y and the route X, U_X, U_Y, Y along the dashed arrows and the dashed double arrow. def:p16-causal-dag (body 23-43) defines only parents, directed paths, descendants and topological orders on the endogenous vertices; ancestors and undirected paths appear only in def:p16-active-path (graphical-separation-adjustment.tex 23-63), again only between endogenous vertices. The source's solid-or-dashed path notion (a path through exogenous variables or through a dashed double arrow) and its Fig. 1(b) two-path example are stated nowhere on the route; body 112-122 and 177-182 translate the source's arrows and double arrows but not its paths.

components.gap: Pearl sec. 3.1, p. 105: the historical claim that Wright's major contribution, besides the language of path diagrams, was a set of graphical rules for writing down the covariance of any pair of observed variables in terms of path coefficients and error covariances, so that (3) and (4) can be written immediately; and the methodological remark that these relations can also be derived from the equations but that for large models algebraic methods obscure the origin of the derived quantities. Body 139-143 only names (3) and (4) as Wright's covariance relations and derives them algebraically in thm:p15-w02c-p15-009-linear-effect; no graphical covariance rule and no comparison with algebraic derivation appears anywhere on the route. Also omitted: Pearl's p. 110 framing that his statement that structural equations say nothing about E(Y | X = x) is made against persistent confusion in the literature (his note 15); body 806-811 reports the statement without this claim about the literature.

components.gap: Pearl sec. 3.1, p. 106, inside the cited secs. 3.1-3.2.3, on the chain of Fig. 2(a): causal assumptions are untestable one at a time while their sum often has testable implications; the chain encodes seven causal assumptions, one per missing arrow or missing double arrow, which together imply that Z is unassociated with Y in every stratum of X, an implication read off the diagram by d-separation (Pearl 1988). The page then illustrates d-separation on the chain's diagram with its disturbances: U_Z -> Z -> X -> Y is blocked by {Z} and by {X}, giving the independencies printed as U_X indep Y | Z and U_Z indep Y | X for every parametrization; U_Z -> Z -> X <- U_X is blocked by the empty set but not by {Y}, so U_Z indep U_X holds while U_Z indep U_X | Y may fail; this collider behaviour is Berkson's paradox (Berkson 1946), with the example of two independent coins made dependent by the report that at least one shows a tail. It closes with the claim that d-separation independencies are the main opening through which such models face nonexperimental data, almost all tests able to invalidate the model being entailed by them, and its note 7 on dormant independences (Shpitser and Pearl 2008). None of this is in def:p16-causal-chain (body 692-733), its commentary (735-770) or elsewhere on the route: the chain's independence of Z and Y given X is never stated (thm:p16-finite-global-markov would yield it), and there is no illustration, collider or Berkson discussion. Only Definition 1 itself is treated, in def:p16-active-path, which cites p. 106 for that definition alone.

components.gap: Lauritzen, inside the cited pp. 65-68: (1) p. 65, the claim introducing Theorem 2.44 that, in contrast to the undirected case, the directed Markov properties are equivalent without further regularity assumptions; the handbook says no positivity or intersection is used (body 209-211) but never states the contrast with undirected graphs. (2) p. 68: a Bayesian network defined by structural equations need not have a density with respect to any product measure, but when it has one the results can be strengthened; the page defines the recursive density factorization (F), gives Proposition 2.51 (F holds exactly when the kernels are conditional densities; proof left to the reader as Exercise 2.8), Lemma 2.52 (F gives a factorization over the moral graph and the global Markov property relative to it), the remark that F implies the recursive kernel factorization R, and Theorem 2.53 (under a density with respect to a product measure, F, R, G, L and O are equivalent). Only the first sentence is covered, by the singular chain of thm:p16-measurable-graph-examples; body 5-8 merely says the source treats densities separately as a special case. Property (F), Proposition 2.51, Lemma 2.52 and Theorem 2.53 are not stated or proved anywhere on the route for a product-measure density; the finite counting-measure implication from factorization to the global property (thm:p16-finite-global-markov) covers neither the general variant nor its converse.

duties.duty: ED26-P16-CH-measurable-causal-graphs-C002 (partial): The status is proved=annex:p16.measurable-ci-calculus, but the full proof is missing for the clause 'Measurable functions may be applied to either independent tuple, also using the conditioning tuple as an argument' (body measurable-causal-graphs.tex 47-48). Its only argument is a one-clause sketch at annex 53-56: 'by pushing forward the conditional product kernels at each z'. Nothing shows that the regular conditional law of (g(X,Z),h(Y,Z)) given Z=z is the image of the conditional product law at z. The substitution identity of thm:p15-kernel-joint-measure that would give this is neither used nor cited, and the proof never returns from that identity to the product-test definition. The Z-free case, both equivalences and the four semigraphoid properties are fully argued.
duties.note: Now argued in full at annex 55-147: the Z-free case, then a kernel pi for (X,Y) given Z with one null set N where it is the product of its marginals, the image kernel rho shown to be a regular conditional law of (g(X,Z),h(Y,Z)) given Z by thm:p15-kernel-joint-measure (substitution identity), the product form of rho(z,.) off N, and the return to the product-test definition via Fubini.

duties.duty: ED26-P16-CH-measurable-causal-graphs-C005 (partial): The status is proved=annex:p16.measurable-kernel-randomization, but the full proof is missing for the 'Consequently' assertion (body 90-94): every finite standard Borel kernel model has a representation X_v=F_v(X_pa(v),U_v) with mutually independent uniform U_v. Annex 157-160 says only 'Topological evaluation and successive conditioning show that its joint law is the kernel law'. It does not show that U_v is independent of the predecessors already constructed, that K_v(X_pa(v),.) is therefore their conditional law, or that induction identifies the joint law with P_K. The matching argument later at annex 508-513 is not invoked. The single-kernel realization (112-155) and the non-uniqueness example (160-166) are complete.
duties.note: Now argued in full at annex 246-318: realization identity for each F_v, independent uniform coordinates on (0,1)^N, and an induction proving independence of U_{v_k} from the constructed predecessors, that K_{v_k}(X_pa,.) is their regular conditional law, and equality of the prefix laws with the stages of P_K by agreement on rectangles.

duties.duty: ED26-P16-CH-measurable-causal-graphs-C010 (partial): The status is proved=annex:p16.measurable-response-component, but the full proof is missing for the stated consequence (body 304-307): one conditional product law of (R,B) given C licenses integration of the whole family at a measurable random parameter depending on (B,C). Annex 567-573 is a two-sentence sketch. It does not derive L(R|B,C)=L(R|C) as kernels from R independent of B given C, and it does not substitute the random parameter into F via thm:p15-kernel-joint-measure. Separately, annex 537-538 ('by the separation hypothesis') relies, without stating or citing them, on two facts: exposing private roots preserves d-separation (stated only later, at 580-581) and the moral-separation bridge. The pointwise representation and R independent of B given C are argued (545-565).
duties.note: Now argued in full: annex 869-875 cites thm:p15-w02c-p15-009-root-exposure (proved at 834-860) and thm:p16-moral-separation-bridge; 894-927 proves R indep B given C; 929-947 derives L(R|B,C)=L(R|C) as kernels from the first CI equivalence; 949-976 substitutes the random parameter via thm:p15-kernel-joint-measure and the tower property; 978-985 treats integrable signed tests.

duties.duty: ED26-P16-CH-measurable-causal-graphs-C012 (partial): The status is proved=annex:p16.measurable-mediation-fields, but the proof of item 1 (body 364-365) is incomplete. In the cross-world field, annex 610-611 claims 'The mediator tuple in this auxiliary model is exactly M_b, by topological evaluation on its restored ancestors'. For that, every exposure child that is an ancestor of a mediator must lie outside D_Y; annex 607-608 gives exposure input a to every exposure child in D_Y. The listed 'exact graph facts' (594-605) put into D_M only the heads of restored edges and their parents. No step places the other exposure children among the mediator ancestors in D_M, so the construction of M_b, and with it R_0 independent of M_b given C, is not fully argued. The claim at 613-615 that every vertex needed for Y belongs to D_Y is likewise only asserted. Items 2 and 3 and the reference-mediator law are argued.
duties.note: Now argued in full at annex 1006-1167: Fact 1 places every exposure descendant that is a mediator ancestor in D_M, Facts 2-3 show the restored graph H_1 keeps the same ancestral set and the component D_Y, Fact 4 fixes C, Fact 5 proves the auxiliary mediator tuple is M_b, Fact 6 proves the auxiliary response is Y_{a,m} with every vertex needed for Y in D_Y, and the conclusion gives R_0 indep M_b given C with F_0 and R_0 free of b.
